title: One function, asked many times

prereqs.why: The exercise is to write one predicate function and call it from a loop, which is the shape of most real code.
There is a loop inside the function and a loop outside it, and keeping them straight is half the work.
An early return out of the inner loop is the idiomatic way to write a predicate.

statement:
Read two integers `a` and `b` with `a <= b`. Print how many primes are in the
inclusive range `a` to `b`, then the largest one, or `none` if there are no
primes in range.

```
input:   10 20        input:   1 1         input:   24 28
output:  count 4      output:  count 0     output:  count 0
         largest 19            largest none         largest none
```

The primes between 10 and 20 are 11, 13, 17 and 19.

### The point of the problem

Write the predicate as its own function:

```cpp
bool isPrime(int n);
```

and then the main loop is a sentence: *for each number in range, if it is prime,
count it and remember it.* The divisibility logic lives in one place, and the
loop that uses it never has to know how primality is decided.

That separation is the whole exercise. A version with the trial division
inlined into the range loop has two nested loops sharing variables, and the
first thing you will want to change - testing fewer divisors - becomes risky
instead of local.

### A definition worth getting exactly right

A prime is a whole number greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and
itself. So:

- `2` is prime - the only even prime
- `1` is **not** prime
- `0` and negatives are **not** prime

Each of those is a hidden test, because each is a line of code.

### Boundary cases

`a == b`, so the range holds one number. A range with no primes at all. A range
starting below 2, including negatives. `2` on its own. `a = b = 2`. Ranges where
the largest prime is the last number and where it is the first.

### Platform assumptions

`a` and `b` fit in a 32-bit `int` and `b` is at most 100000, so trial division
up to the square root is far inside any time limit. `i * i <= n` is used rather
than `i <= sqrt(n)`, and with `n` under 100000 the product cannot overflow a
32-bit `int`.
hints: Start the predicate with the exclusions: `if (n < 2) return false;`. Getting 0, 1 and the negatives out of the way first means the loop below can assume a number worth testing.
Trial division: for each `i` from 2 upward, if `n % i == 0` then `n` is not prime, so `return false` immediately. If the loop finishes without finding a divisor, `return true`.

Stop the divisor loop at `i * i <= n`, not at `i < n`. If `n` has a divisor larger than its square root, it must also have the matching one below it - so there is nothing left to find above that point.
